claim: Direction-selectivity in the mammalian retina is thought to originate in the dendrites of GABAergic/cholinergic starburst amacrine cells, where it is first observed.
source: In the mammalian retina, direction-selectivity is thought to originate in the dendrites of GABAergic/cholinergic starburst amacrine cells, where it is first observed.
evidence: This is a statement about established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Direction selectivity in downstream ganglion cells remains remarkably unaffected when starburst dendrites are rendered non-directional using a conditional GABAA α2 receptor knockout mouse with optogenetics.
source: However, here we demonstrate that direction selectivity in downstream ganglion cells remains remarkably unaffected when starburst dendrites are rendered non-directional, using a novel strategy combining a conditional GABAA α2 receptor knockout mouse with optogenetics.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Temporal asymmetries between excitation and inhibition arise from the differential connectivity patterns of starburst cholinergic and GABAergic synapses to ganglion cells.
source: We show that temporal asymmetries between excitation/inhibition, arising from the differential connectivity patterns of starburst cholinergic and GABAergic synapses to ganglion cells, form the basis for a parallel mechanism generating direction selectivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Temporal asymmetries between excitation and inhibition form the basis for a parallel mechanism generating direction selectivity.
source: We show that temporal asymmetries between excitation/inhibition, arising from the differential connectivity patterns of starburst cholinergic and GABAergic synapses to ganglion cells, form the basis for a parallel mechanism generating direction selectivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Two distinct mechanisms work in a coordinated way to refine direction selectivity as the stimulus crosses the ganglion cell's receptive field.
source: We further demonstrate that these distinct mechanisms work in a coordinated way to refine direction selectivity as the stimulus crosses the ganglion cell's receptive field.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Precise spatiotemporal patterns of inhibition and excitation that determine directional responses in ganglion cells are shaped by two 'core' mechanisms, both arising from distinct specializations of the starburst network.
source: Thus, precise spatiotemporal patterns of inhibition and excitation that determine directional responses in ganglion cells are shaped by two 'core' mechanisms, both arising from distinct specializations of the starburst network.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: The direction-selective circuit in the retina is one of the most well-defined circuits in the mammalian brain.
source: The direction-selective (DS) circuit in the retina is arguably one of the most well-defined circuits in the mammalian brain (reviewed by Mauss et al., 2017; Vaney et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Direction is encoded by output DS ganglion cells (DSGCs).
source: In this circuit, direction is encoded by output DS ganglion cells (DSGCs), whose response properties are shaped by DS inputs arising from GABAergic/cholinergic starburst amacrine cells (starbursts) and non-DS inputs from glutamatergic bipolar cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the DS circuit.

claim: DSGC response properties are shaped by DS inputs arising from GABAergic/cholinergic starburst amacrine cells and non-DS inputs from glutamatergic bipolar cells.
source: In this circuit, direction is encoded by output DS ganglion cells (DSGCs), whose response properties are shaped by DS inputs arising from GABAergic/cholinergic starburst amacrine cells (starbursts) and non-DS inputs from glutamatergic bipolar cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the DS circuit, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The fundamental mechanisms underlying direction selectivity at the level of starbursts and DSGCs remain to be fully elucidated despite comprehensive connectomic analysis and decades of physiological investigations.
source: However, despite comprehensive connectomic analysis of the circuit (Briggman et al., 2011; Ding et al., 2016) and many decades of physiological investigations, the fundamental mechanisms underlying direction selectivity, both at the level of starbursts and DSGCs remain to be fully elucidated.
evidence: This statement acknowledges the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The first points in the visual system where direction selectivity is observed are the radiating dendrites of starbursts.
source: The first points in the visual system where direction selectivity is observed are the radiating dendrites of starbursts (Euler et al., 2002), which release GABA and acetylcholine (ACh) (O'Malley and Masland, 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Starburst dendrites release GABA and acetylcholine (ACh).
source: The first points in the visual system where direction selectivity is observed are the radiating dendrites of starbursts (Euler et al., 2002), which release GABA and acetylcholine (ACh) (O'Malley and Masland, 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Initial studies emphasized mechanisms based on intrinsic properties of starburst dendrites to explain direction selectivity.
source: To explain direction selectivity, initial studies emphasized mechanisms that were based on intrinsic properties of starburst dendrites (Gavrikov et al., 2006; Hausselt et al., 2007; Tukker et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent studies have proposed two distinct network mechanisms for direction selectivity in starburst dendrites.
source: In contrast, more recent studies have proposed two distinct network mechanisms.
evidence: This statement introduces recent research findings.

claim: The first network mechanism relies on inhibition within the dense array of starburst cells, where dendrites of neighboring starbursts with opposite directional preferences mutually inhibit each other.
source: The first relies on inhibition within the dense array of starburst cells, where dendrites of neighboring starbursts with opposite directional preferences mutually inhibit each other. This ensures that dendrites pointing in a particular direction are maximally activated as the moving stimulus sequentially activates the starbursts (Ding et al., 2016; Lee and Zhou, 2006; Münch and Werblin, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The second network mechanism relies on the specific wiring of temporally distinct bipolar cells along the proximal-distal axis of the starburst dendrite.
source: The second network mechanism relies on the specific wiring of temporally distinct bipolar cells along the proximal-distal axis of the starburst dendrite. This arrangement results in an optimal summation of inputs when the stimulus moves centrifugally (from soma-to dendrite) along the starbursts dendrites (Fransen and Borghuis, 2017; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neither of the two network mechanisms appears to be critically required for generating DS in the context of simple spot/grating stimuli.
source: When tested experimentally, however, neither of these mechanisms appears to be critically required for generating DS, at least in the context of simple spot/grating stimuli (Chen et al., 2016; Sethuramanujam et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Starbursts play an obligatory role in generating direction selectivity in downstream DSGCs.
source: Starbursts play an obligatory role in generating direction selectivity in downstream DSGCs (Vlasits et al., 2014; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Starbursts provide the neural substrate for a powerful GABAergic 'null' inhibition that is required for the generation of DS responses in ganglion cells.
source: They provide the neural substrate for a powerful GABAergic 'null' inhibition that is required for the generation of DS responses in ganglion cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the DS circuit, also illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Null inhibition relies on both the DS properties of starburst dendrites and a specific 'anti-parallel' wiring scheme.
source: Null inhibition relies on both the DS properties of starburst dendrites and also a specific 'anti-parallel' wiring scheme (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the DS circuit, also illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Only starbursts with somas displaced to the null-side of the DSGC's receptive field make synaptic connections with DSGCs.
source: Only starbursts with somas displaced to the null-side of the DSGC's receptive field (i.e. the side from which null-stimuli enter the receptive field) make synaptic connections with DSGCs (Briggman et al., 2011; Brombas et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016; Fried et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2010; Yonehara et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Excitatory inputs to DSGCs arising from bipolar cells are non-DS.
source: By contrast, excitatory inputs to DSGCs arising from bipolar cells are non-DS (Park et al., 2014; Yonehara et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A well-accepted model proposes that direction selectivity in DSGCs is largely inherited from starburst dendrites, contingent on the DS release of GABA.
source: Together, these findings have given rise to a well-accepted model in which direction selectivity in DSGCs is largely inherited from starburst dendrites, contingent on the DS release of GABA (Figure 1C) (reviewed by Mauss et al., 2017; Vaney et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement describes a well-accepted model in the field, supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Starbursts co-release ACh in addition to GABA.
source: However, in addition to GABA, starbursts also co-release ACh (O'Malley and Masland, 1989), which mediates fast excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in DSGCs via the activation of nicotinic ACh (nACh) receptors (Brombas et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2010; Pei et al., 2015; Sethuramanujam et al., 2016; Taylor and Smith, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ACh mediates fast excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in DSGCs via the activation of nicotinic ACh (nACh) receptors.
source: However, in addition to GABA, starbursts also co-release ACh (O'Malley and Masland, 1989), which mediates fast excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in DSGCs via the activation of nicotinic ACh (nACh) receptors (Brombas et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2010; Pei et al., 2015; Sethuramanujam et al., 2016; Taylor and Smith, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cholinergic signals appear to be more symmetrical at the level of DSGCs, giving rise to the notion it modulates the amplitude of DSGC responses.
source: Unlike GABA, however, cholinergic signals appear to be more symmetrical at the level of DSGCs, giving rise to the notion it modulates the amplitude of DSGC responses (Ariel and Daw, 1982; Amthor et al., 1996; Chiao and Masland, 2002; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent voltage-clamp recordings reveal amplitude differences between preferred and null-evoked cholinergic currents, suggesting that ACh may directly contribute to direction selectivity.
source: Recent voltage-clamp recordings on the other hand, reveal amplitude differences between preferred and null-evoked cholinergic currents (Figure 1C), suggesting that ACh may directly contribute to direction selectivity (Lee et al., 2010; Pei et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The mechanisms underlying DS cholinergic excitation remain unknown.
source: However, the mechanisms underlying DS cholinergic excitation remain unknown.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Cholinergic inputs arise from starbursts surrounding DSGCs from all directions, in sharp contrast to GABA inputs.
source: Elegant starburst/DSGC paired recordings demonstrate that cholinergic inputs arise from starbursts surrounding DSGCs from all directions, in sharp contrast to GABA inputs (Figure 1A) (Brombas et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2010; Yonehara et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Cholinergic excitation is presumed to be mediated by paracrine mechanisms that are agnostic to the specific connectivity.
source: Given the asymmetric anatomical wiring of the starbursts and DSGCs (Figure 1B), it is presumed that cholinergic excitation is mediated by paracrine mechanisms that are agnostic to the specific connectivity (Briggman et al., 2011; Brombas et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The differential functional connectivity of spatially offset GABA and ACh signals produces excitation-inhibition (E/I) timing differences that generate direction selectivity.
source: Building on these findings, in this study we hypothesized that the differential functional connectivity of spatially offset GABA and ACh signals produces excitation-inhibition (E/I) timing differences that generate direction selectivity, as originally envisioned (Koch et al., 1982; Taylor et al., 2000; Torre and Poggio, 1978).
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study, supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: E/I timing differences could serve as a parallel 'hard-wired' DS mechanism that does not necessarily require DS starburst output.
source: This could serve as a parallel 'hard-wired' DS mechanisms that does not necessarily require DS starburst output (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Temporal E/I asymmetries have often been noted in the literature, but their impact has been difficult to assess because they are always associated with changes in E/I amplitude ratio.
source: It is important to note that temporal E/I asymmetries have often been noted in the literature, but their impact has been difficult to assess, as they are always associated with changes in E/I amplitude ratio (Figure 1D) (Fried et al., 2005; Kostadinov and Sanes, 2015; Pei et al., 2015; Sethuramanujam et al., 2016; Taylor and Vaney, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Blocking cholinergic inputs does not appear to affect the ability of DSGCs to encode direction.
source: Further, blocking cholinergic inputs, which is expected to decrease E/I timing differences arising from the above-mentioned specific wiring of starburst ACh/GABA synapses (Figure 1D), does not appear to affect the ability of DSGCs to encode direction (Ariel and Daw, 1982; Kittila and Massey, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Robust direction selectivity is observed in instances where E/I temporal offsets are not apparent.
source: It has also been shown that robust direction selectivity is observed in instances where E/I temporal offsets are not apparent (Taylor and Vaney, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Modeling studies suggest that E/I temporal offsets play a negligible role in DS computation in the context of E/I amplitude modulation.
source: Additionally, modeling studies suggest that E/I temporal offsets play a negligible role in this computation in the context of the E/I amplitude modulation (Schachter et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The contribution of E/I temporal offsets to direction coding by DSGCs are generally neglected.
source: Thus, the contribution of E/I temporal offsets to direction coding by DSGCs are generally neglected.
evidence: This statement summarizes the current state of the field.

claim: Using a novel combination of optogenetics/mouse KO technology/pharmacology, the authors render starburst output non-DS for the first time.
source: Here, we describe two major advancements that better our understanding of the DS circuitry in the mouse retina. First, using a novel combination of optogenetics/mouse KO technology/pharmacology, we render starburst output non-DS for the first time.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Blocking starburst DS had a surprisingly weak effect on direction selectivity in ganglion cells.
source: Second, we found that blocking starburst DS had a surprisingly weak effect on direction selectivity in ganglion cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: A second 'core' DS mechanism relies on E/I temporal offsets.
source: This demonstrates the existence of a second 'core' DS mechanism, which we demonstrate relies on E/I temporal offsets.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Changes in E/I ratios or timing differences are each sufficient to drive robust DS responses in ganglion cells.
source: Interestingly, while changes in E/I ratios or timing differences are each sufficient to drive robust DS responses in ganglion cells, these mechanisms contribute to distinct phases of the DSGC response, ensuring that direction is computed rapidly and with high fidelity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: E/I ratio and timing mechanisms contribute to distinct phases of the DSGC response, ensuring that direction is computed rapidly and with high fidelity.
source: Interestingly, while changes in E/I ratios or timing differences are each sufficient to drive robust DS responses in ganglion cells, these mechanisms contribute to distinct phases of the DSGC response, ensuring that direction is computed rapidly and with high fidelity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: The DS output of starbursts measured as IPSCs in DSGCs was similar in Gabra2 KO mice and wild type mice.
source: Consistent with these findings, we found the DS output of the starbursts measured as inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in DSGCs, was similar in Gabra2 KO mice and wild type mice. This was quantified using a direction selectivity index (DSI; calculated as the normalized vector sum of responses measured across eight directions; Wt = 0.33 ± 0.019, n = 6; KO = 0.28 ± 0.022; n = 6; data are presented as mean ± SEM; Figure 2A,B,E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Robust DS output was observed in the absence of bipolar cell input when starbursts were directly stimulated using optogenetics.
source: Arguing against excitatory network mechanisms (Fransen and Borghuis, 2017; Kim et al., 2014), robust DS output was observed in the absence of bipolar cell input, when the starbursts were directly stimulated using optogenetics (Figure 2C,E & F; Sethuramanujam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Combining approaches to block both inhibitory and excitatory network DS mechanisms led to the near-complete block of the asymmetry in responses mediated by starburst cells.
source: Remarkably, combining these two approaches to block both inhibitory and excitatory network DS mechanisms, led to the near-complete block of the asymmetry in responses mediated by starburst cells, i.e. the amplitudes of inhibitory inputs evoked by optogenetic stimulation of starbursts in the Gabra2 KO background were nearly equal for preferred and null-direction motion (DSI = 0.07 ± 0.02, n = 7; Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The requirement to block both excitatory and inhibitory network mechanisms suggests that they work in parallel to shape DS responses in starburst dendrites.
source: The requirement to block both the excitatory (Fransen and Borghuis, 2017; Kim et al., 2014) and inhibitory network mechanisms (Ding et al., 2016; Lee and Zhou, 2006; Münch and Werblin, 2006) suggest that they work in parallel to shape DS responses in starburst dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: DSGCs in Gabra2 KO mice continued to exhibit robust spiking responses when starburst output was rendered non-DS.
source: Contrary to this notion, we found that DSGCs in Gabra2 KO mice continued to exhibit robust spiking responses when starburst output was rendered non-DS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Spiking responses in DSGCs were robustly tuned for direction when starburst output was rendered non-DS, similar to control conditions.
source: Strikingly, these spiking responses were robustly tuned for direction similar to control conditions (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The direction encoded was the same under conditions in which starburst output was DS or non-DS.
source: While the direction encoded was the same under conditions in which starburst output was DS or non-DS (Figure 3A), we did observe a significant reduction in the duration of the DSGC's spiking response (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A significant reduction in the duration of the DSGC's spiking response was observed when starburst output was rendered non-DS.
source: While the direction encoded was the same under conditions in which starburst output was DS or non-DS (Figure 3A), we did observe a significant reduction in the duration of the DSGC's spiking response (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Starbursts must utilize an alternate mechanism to confer direction selectivity upon DSGCs in the absence of amplitude modulation of inhibitory inputs.
source: Since starbursts are critically required for DS computation (Vlasits et al., 2014; Yoshida et al., 2001), it follows that they must utilize an alternate mechanism to confer direction selectivity upon DSGCs, in the absence of amplitude modulation of inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and previous research.

claim: The direction tuning properties of the DSGC remain unchanged when starburst output is rendered non-DS, indicating that the second DS mechanism is well-aligned to the classical mechanism.
source: In addition, the finding that the direction tuning properties of the DSGC remains unchanged when starburst output is rendered non-DS (Figure 3B,D), indicates that this second DS mechanism is well-aligned to the classical mechanism relying on the direction selectivity of starburst dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 3.

claim: E/I temporal offsets in the Gabra2 KO were exquisitely tuned for direction.
source: When we examined the onset latencies for GABA and ACh in the Gabra2 KO, we found E/I temporal offsets were exquisitely tuned for direction (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The magnitude of the E/I temporal offsets provided a good indication of the DSGC's preferred-direction when compared to its spiking responses.
source: The magnitude of the offsets provided a good indication of the DSGC's preferred-direction when compared to its spiking responses measured prior to the voltage-clamp experiments (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Temporal asymmetries in E/I onsets alone can drive direction selectivity in ganglion cells.
source: These results provided strong evidence that temporal asymmetries in E/I onsets alone can drive direction selectivity in ganglion cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Temporal asymmetries arise from the starburst network itself through a differential functional connectivity of cholinergic/GABAergic synapses to DSGCs.
source: Moreover, since temporal asymmetries are observed under conditions in which photoreceptor/glutamate receptors are blocked, it indicates that they arise from the starburst network itself, through a differential functional connectivity of cholinergic/GABAergic synapses to DSGCs (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Temporal asymmetries were observed under natural conditions when responses were driven by photoreceptors.
source: Temporal asymmetries were also observed under natural conditions, i.e. when responses were driven by photoreceptors (Figure 4E–H), consistent with previous studies (Fried et al., 2002; Kostadinov and Sanes, 2015; Pei et al., 2015; Sethuramanujam et al., 2016; Taylor and Vaney, 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 4, and is consistent with previous research.

claim: The magnitude of the E/I temporal offsets measured under physiological conditions was greatest for preferred-direction motion and progressively decreased as the stimulus direction approached the DSGC's null-direction.
source: Similar to the optogenetic experiments, the magnitude of the E/I temporal offsets measured under physiological conditions (i.e. photoreceptor mediated) was greatest for preferred-direction motion and progressively decreased as the stimulus direction approached the DSGC's null-direction (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The E/I temporal offset tuning was significantly sharper when compared to the tuning of the spiking responses.
source: The E/I temporal offset tuning was significantly sharper when compared to the tuning of the spiking responses, as indicated by the DSI (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The predicted direction based on offsets were almost perfectly aligned with the direction encoded based on the spiking responses.
source: By contrast, the predicted direction based on offsets were almost perfectly aligned with the direction encoded based on the spiking responses (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Blocking nicotinic ACh receptors increased the onset latency for excitation evoked by motion in the preferred-direction and largely abolished the E/I temporal offsets in this direction.
source: Consistent with the notion that E/I temporal offsets arise from a differential transmission of ACh/GABA (Figure 1D), blocking nicotinic ACh (nACh) receptors using a specific antagonist (100 µM hexamethonium) increased the onset latency for excitation evoked by motion in the preferred-direction, and largely abolished the E/I temporal offsets in this direction (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 5.

claim: For null-direction motion, blocking nACh receptors resulted in a negative offset, as the GABAergic inhibition arising from null-side starbursts was no longer balanced by cholinergic inputs but continued to arrive before glutamate inputs.
source: For null-direction motion, blocking these receptors resulted in a negative offset, as the GABAergic inhibition arising from null-side starbursts was no longer balanced by cholinergic inputs but continued to arrive before glutamate inputs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Hexamethonium uniformly reduces the E/I temporal offsets by ~25 ms regardless of direction.
source: Plotting the E/I temporal offsets for all stimulus directions reveals that hexamethonium uniformly reduces the E/I temporal offsets by ~25 ms (average delay = 26 ± 2 ms; n = 8) regardless of direction (Figure 5B,C), consistent with the idea that starbursts make cholinergic connections from all around the DSGC (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ~25 ms delay corresponds to a spatial offset of ~25 μm given the stimulus moved at 1000 μm/s.
source: Given the stimulus moved at 1000 μm/s, this corresponds to a spatial offset of ~25 μm (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Both ACh and GABA signals arising from starburst dendrites are spatially offset relative to glutamate inputs.
source: It is also worth noting that, both ACh and GABA signals arising from starburst dendrites are spatially offset relative to glutamate inputs (Figure 1B,D), unlike the co-extensive glutamatergic/cholinergic receptive fields observed in rabbit retina (Brombas et al., 2017; Fried et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, illustrated in Figure 1, and contrasted with previous research in rabbit retina.

claim: The differential transmission of ACh/GABA produces E/I that are temporally synchronized in the null- but not preferred-direction.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the differential transmission of ACh/GABA produces E/I that are temporally synchronized in the null- but not preferred-direction (Figure 1D and Figure 5A), providing the substrate for a timing based mechanism for generating direction selectivity in ganglion cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In the Gabra2 KO-ChR2, where DS in DSGCs relies solely on temporal E/I offsets, the number of optogenetically evoked spikes decreased as a function of velocity.
source: In the Gabra2 KO-ChR2, where DS in DSGCs relies solely on temporal E/I offsets, the number of optogenetically evoked spikes were found to decrease as a function of velocity, as expected (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Despite the drop in the spike responses at higher stimulus velocities, the direction selectivity was not altered in the Gabra2 KO-ChR2.
source: However, despite the drop in the spike responses at higher stimulus velocities, the direction selectivity was not altered (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The amplitude of E/I temporal offsets measured in the DSGC's preferred direction reduced with velocity, but were still measurable at the highest velocities tested (2400 μm/s).
source: The amplitude of E/I temporal offsets measured in the DSGC's preferred direction reduced with velocity, but were still measurable at the highest velocities tested (2400 μm/s; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The values of the E/I temporal offsets measured at different speeds corresponded to a ~ 30 μm spatial offset between excitatory and inhibitory receptive fields.
source: The values of the E/I temporal offsets measured at different speeds corresponded to a ~ 30 μm spatial offset between excitatory and inhibitory receptive fields (Figure 6B inset).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Addition of nACh receptor antagonists abolished the E/I temporal offsets, confirming that the spatial offsets are mediated by starburst inputs at all velocities.
source: Addition of nACh receptor antagonists (hexamethonium) abolished the E/I temporal offsets, confirming that the spatial offsets are mediated by starburst inputs at all velocities (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: For null-direction motion, E/I were co-activated through most of the velocity range, except for the lower velocities where inhibition tended to lead excitation.
source: Conversely, for null-direction motion, E/I were co-activated through most of the velocity range, except for the lower velocities where inhibition tended to lead excitation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A model DSGC with E/I temporal offsets but constant amplitude ratio generated robust DS responses through most of the velocity range.
source: As with our optogenetic study, for preferred motion, the number of spikes decreased as a function of velocity (Figure 6D), but remained robustly directional through most of velocity range.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At the lowest speed in the model, the DSI decreased because edges moving in the null direction spent considerable time on the excitatory receptive field after inhibition ceased.
source: Only at the lowest speed, where the edges moving in the null direction spent considerable time on the excitatory receptive field after inhibition ceased, the model generated a few null-direction spikes, resulting in a decreased DSI (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The simplified model captures many aspects of the DSGC response properties and supports the idea that the E/I temporal offset mechanism contributes to direction selectivity in ganglion cells over a wide range of velocities.
source: Thus, the simplified model captures many aspects of the DSGC response properties, and supports the idea that the E/I temporal offset mechanism contributes to direction selectivity in ganglion cells over a wide range of velocities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling.

claim: When the spiking responses were averaged over the entire trial, the direction selectivity generated with or without DS inhibition was similar.
source: When the spiking responses were averaged over the entire trial, the direction selectivity generated with or without DS inhibition was similar, and thus the DS mechanisms appear redundant (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: When the DS tuning was examined on a finer time-scale, it showed distinct characteristics in the early and peak phases of the response.
source: However, when the DS tuning was examined on a finer time-scale (Figure 7), it showed distinct characteristics in the early and peak phases of the response, raising the possibility that the two mechanisms operate on distinct time-scales.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 7.

claim: While the direction encoded remained constant throughout the response, the tuning curve broadened as the response approached its peak, resulting in a marked decrease in the DSI.
source: While the direction encoded remained constant throughout the response, the tuning curve broadened as the response approached its peak, resulting in a marked decrease in the DSI (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The initial estimate of direction was more variable compared to that made during the peak of the response.
source: Moreover, the initial estimate of direction was more variable compared to that made during the peak of the response (standard deviation of early and peak responses were 16 ± 20; and 8 ± 20, respectively; Figure 7B,E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The broadening of the tuning curve did not arise simply from a thresholding effect (i.e. an iceberg effect).
source: It is also important to note that the broadening of the tuning curve did not arise simply from a thresholding effect (i.e. an iceberg effect), as the last spikes at the tail end of the response were not sharply tuned (data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: E/I temporal offsets alone resulted in sharper tuning similar to the early responses, but the tuning became broader when E/I ratios were intact, similar to the peak responses.
source: E/I temporal offsets alone resulted in a sharper tuning similar to the early responses in B), but the tuning became broader when E/I ratios were intact, similar to the peak responses in B) (see Figure 7—figure supplement 2 for synaptic currents and spiking responses measured in the model).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The DS mechanisms based on temporal and amplitude asymmetries appear to be complementary, each conferring distinct advantages.
source: Thus, the DS mechanisms based on temporal and amplitude asymmetries appear to be complementary, each conferring distinct advantages: the former enables DSGCs to respond in a direction-selective manner sooner than they would have done otherwise, while the latter enables DSGCs to encode direction with higher fidelity albeit on a slower time scale.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling findings.

claim: Multiple circuit mechanisms serve to generate direction-selectivity at the level of starburst dendrites and in downstream DSGCs.
source: Our experiments using various pharmacological, optogenetic and cell-specific KO strategies to analyse synaptic inputs to DSGCs, suggest that multiple circuit mechanisms serve to generate direction-selectivity at both these points in the DS circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The results help amalgamate divergent views on the mechanisms underlying direction selectivity in starburst dendrites.
source: These results highlight the apparently redundant roles for excitatory and inhibitory network mechanisms and help amalgamate divergent views (Ding et al., 2016; Fransen and Borghuis, 2017; Kim et al., 2014; Lee and Zhou, 2006; Münch and Werblin, 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Two fundamental mechanisms generating DS in DSGCs appear to originate from unique specializations of the starburst network.
source: At the level of DSGCs too, multiple DS mechanisms appear to be in play. Here, two fundamental mechanisms appear to originate from unique specializations of the starburst network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The first mechanism relies on amplitude asymmetries arising from the DS starburst dendrites and asymmetric starburst-DSGC wiring.
source: The first mechanism, which relies on amplitude asymmetries arising from the DS starburst dendrites (Figure 1C) and asymmetric starburst-DSGC wiring (Figure 1B), is well established (reviewed by Mauss et al., 2017; Vaney et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement describes a well-established mechanism in the field, supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The results demonstrate for the first time that E/I temporal offsets are tuned precisely to the DSGC's preferred direction and are alone sufficient to generate direction selective responses in ganglion cells.
source: While E/I temporal offsets have often been noted in the literature (Fried et al., 2005; Kostadinov and Sanes, 2015; Pei et al., 2015; Sethuramanujam et al., 2016; Sivyer et al., 2010; Taylor and Vaney, 2002), our results demonstrate for the first time that they are tuned precisely to the DSGC's preferred direction, and are alone sufficient to generate direction selective responses in ganglion cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Recent studies using voltage-clamp techniques have shown the amplitude of the cholinergic signal to vary according to direction.
source: Recent studies using voltage-clamp techniques have also shown the amplitude of the cholinergic signal to vary according to direction (Lee et al., 2010; Pei et al., 2015; Park et al., 2014; Sethuramanujam et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dynamic changes in the inhibitory conductance could lead to serious voltage-clamp errors and affect estimates of the relative peak amplitude of cholinergic input in the preferred and null direction.
source: However, these results need to be interpreted with caution. Dynamic changes in the inhibitory conductance could lead to serious voltage-clamp errors and estimates of the relative peak amplitude of cholinergic input in the preferred and null direction (Poleg-Polsky and Diamond, 2011; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research and data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The E/I offset mechanisms generating DS do not require amplitude changes in cholinergic inputs.
source: Importantly, the E/I offset mechanisms generating DS described here do not require amplitude changes in cholinergic inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Cholinergic, GABAergic and glutamatergic synapses are made relatively uniformly throughout the DSGC receptive field and are thought to constitute repeating dendritic DS subunits.
source: It is also worth noting that cholinergic, GABAergic and glutamatergic synapses are made relatively uniformly throughout the DSGC receptive field and are thought to constitute repeating dendritic DS subunits (Barlow and Levick, 1965; Taylor et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Temporal asymmetries are most apparent at response onset in recordings made from the DSGC soma, but are likely present throughout the dendritic tree.
source: Thus, although the temporal asymmetries are most apparent at response onset in our recordings made from the DSGC soma, they are likely present throughout the dendritic tree.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and knowledge of the circuit.

claim: Classic models suggested that DS responses in ganglion cells were based on E/I timing differences before the discovery of DS in starburst dendrites.
source: Before the discovery of DS in starburst dendrites, classic models suggested that DS responses in ganglion cells were based on E/I timing differences (Koch et al., 1982; Taylor et al., 2000; Torre and Poggio, 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies have speculated that an intermediary cell in the inner and/or outer retina may control E/I timing differences at DSGCs.
source: Previous studies have speculated that an intermediary cell in the inner and/or outer retina may control E/I timing differences at DSGCs (Rivlin-Etzion et al., 2012; Taylor and Vaney, 2002; Vlasits et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Another study found that perturbing starburst cell morphology led to parallel changes in E/I amplitude ratio and E/I temporal offsets suggesting that these processes may be inextricably linked.
source: In contrast, another study found that perturbing starburst cell morphology led to parallel changes in E/I amplitude ratio and E/I temporal offsets suggesting that these processes may be inextricably linked (Kostadinov and Sanes, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The temporal asymmetries in E/I are a natural consequence of the asymmetric/symmetric GABAergic/cholinergic connectivity of starburst cells to DSGCs.
source: Our combined results from optogenetic, pharmacological and modelling experiments indicate that the temporal asymmetries in E/I are a natural consequence of the asymmetric/symmetric GABAergic/cholinergic connectivity of starburst cells to DSGCs (Figure 1; Chen et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2010; Yonehara et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Null-side starbursts extend the inhibitory receptive fields of DSGCs during null motion, producing a more powerful inhibition.
source: In this scheme, null-side starbursts extend the inhibitory receptive fields of DSGCs during null motion, producing a more powerful inhibition (Fried et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cholinergic excitation provided by preferred-side starbursts enable DSGCs to respond sooner to the moving edge than they would otherwise.
source: Conversely, cholinergic excitation provided by preferred-side starbursts enable DSGCs to respond sooner to the moving edge than they would otherwise.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The degree to which cholinergic inputs advance the response is proportional to stimulus velocity, corresponding to a fixed spatial offset ~30 µm.
source: We found that the degree to which cholinergic inputs advance the response is proportional to stimulus velocity, corresponding to a fixed spatial offset ~30 µm.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: In mouse retina, starbursts receive excitatory and inhibitory inputs on proximal dendrites but release transmitter from varicosities located on their distal dendrites.
source: In mouse retina, starbursts receive excitatory and inhibitory inputs on proximal dendrites but release transmitter from varicosities located on their distal dendrites (Ding et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2014; Vlasits et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mapping the receptive fields of individual starburst varicosities using Ca2+ imaging shows them to be displaced by ~25 µm towards the soma.
source: Mapping the receptive fields of individual starburst varicosities using Ca2+ imaging shows them to be displaced by ~25 µm towards the soma (Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The extent to which cholinergic inputs expand the receptive field of the DSGC is well predicted by the input/output properties of starburst dendrites.
source: Thus, the extent to which cholinergic inputs expand the receptive field of the DSGC is well predicted by the input/output properties of starburst dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and previous research.

claim: Despite being generated by paracrine mechanisms, the distance over which ACh spreads appears relatively limited.
source: The dimensions of the cholinergic receptive fields also indicate that despite being generated by paracrine mechanisms (which loosens the constraints set by the asymmetrical starburst-DSGC 'hard-wiring'; Figure 1B) (Briggman et al., 2011; Brombas et al., 2017), the distance over which ACh spreads appears relatively limited.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In rabbit retina, cholinergic excitation is co-extensive with the glutamatergic receptive field and does not appear to extend the DSGC's receptive field beyond the dendritic field.
source: In contrast to our findings, in rabbit retina, cholinergic excitation is co-extensive with the glutamatergic receptive field and does not appear to extend the DSGC's receptive field beyond the dendritic field (Brombas et al., 2017; Fried et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2010; Yang and Masland, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Static stimuli employed in previous studies to measure the receptive field properties of DSGCs may not optimally stimulate starbursts and therefore fail to reveal cholinergic excitation.
source: One reason for this could be that static stimuli employed in previous studies to measure the receptive field properties of DSGCs do not optimally stimulate starbursts, and therefore fail to reveal cholinergic excitation (Fried et al., 2005; Yang and Masland, 1992).
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for differences between studies.

claim: In rabbit retina, the release of ACh may require a stronger stimulation of the starbursts, causing a delay in the release of ACh, making it co-extensive with glutamate input.
source: Alternatively, in rabbit retina, the release of ACh may require a stronger stimulation of the starbursts (Lee et al., 2010). This causes a delay in the release of ACh, making it co-extensive with glutamate input (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for differences between studies, supported by a citation.

claim: Under conditions where inhibition is blocked and starburst dendrites are more strongly stimulated, cholinergic inputs do provide lateral excitation in rabbit retina.
source: Indeed, under conditions where inhibition is blocked and starburst dendrites are more strongly stimulated, cholinergic inputs do provide lateral excitation (Fried et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2010; Vaney et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The findings have given rise to the notion that the role of ACh is modulatory, in contrast to what was observed in mouse retina.
source: Together, these findings have given rise to the notion that the role of ACh is modulatory (Ariel and Daw, 1982; Amthor et al., 1996; Chiao and Masland, 2002; Lee et al., 2010; but see Pei et al., 2015), in contrast to what we observed in mouse retina.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The demonstration that the parallel circuit mechanisms driving direction selectivity in ganglion cells are individually dispensable necessitates a re-evaluation of conclusions drawn from previous studies.
source: The demonstration that the parallel circuit mechanisms driving direction selectivity in ganglion cells are individually dispensable necessitates a re-evaluation of the conclusions drawn from a multitude of studies carried out over the last several decades that considered a single 'core' DS mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Numerous studies over the last forty years have found that blocking cholinergic receptors does not affect direction selectivity in DSGCs.
source: For example, numerous studies over the last forty years have found that blocking cholinergic receptors does not affect direction selectivity in DSGCs and have taken this to mean that ACh does not play an integral role in DS (reviewed by Mauss et al., 2017; Vaney et al., 2012), but rather provides an additional source of non-directional excitation to boost DSGC responses (Brombas et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2010), that is especially important under limiting conditions (Sethuramanujam et al., 2016; Sethuramanujam et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles and previous research.

claim: The results indicate that ACh signals are highly directional, not so much in their amplitudes as previously envisioned, but rather by virtue of their relative timing with inhibition.
source: In sharp contrast, our results here indicate that in fact ACh signals (unlike glutamate signals) are highly directional, not so much in their amplitudes as previously envisioned (Chen et al., 2016; Grzywacz et al., 1998; Grzywacz et al., 1997; Lee et al., 2010; Pei et al., 2015), but rather by virtue of their relative timing with inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Cholinergic excitation and GABAergic inhibition are relatively imbalanced (or out of phase) during preferred-direction motion, but extremely well-balanced (or in phase) during null-direction motion.
source: Cholinergic excitation and GABAergic inhibition are relatively imbalanced (or out of phase) during preferred-direction motion, but extremely well-balanced (or in phase) during null-direction motion, which is important for the computation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Under low contrast conditions, glutamate appears to be mediated by NMDA receptors and plays an important role modulating cholinergic excitation.
source: Previously, we have shown that under low contrast conditions, glutamate appears to be mediated by NMDA receptors (Sethuramanujam et al., 2016; Sethuramanujam et al., 2017) and play an important role modulating cholinergic excitation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: Under high contrast conditions, glutamate signaling is mediated by both AMPA and NMDA receptors.
source: Under high contrast conditions, as we have used here, glutamate signaling is mediated by both AMPA and NMDA receptors.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Glutamate input is relatively delayed and therefore makes the DSGC's preferred response more sustained.
source: Glutamate input is relatively delayed and therefore makes the DSGC's preferred response more sustained.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: AMPA inputs are non-directional and are expected to broaden the DS tuning curve by changing the E/I ratio across direction.
source: Moreover, since AMPA inputs are non-directional they are expected to broaden the DS tuning curve, by changing the E/I ratio across direction (Poleg-Polsky and Diamond, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and previous research.

claim: A measurable broadening of the real DSGC tuning curves is noted at higher contrasts, although these effects are relatively small.
source: Indeed, a measurable broadening of the real DSGC tuning curves is noted at higher contrasts, although these effects are relatively small (Sethuramanujam et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: The E/I ratio is predicted to change over the duration of directional light responses given the difference in receptive fields between bipolar and starburst inputs to DSGCs.
source: Additionally, given the difference in receptive fields between bipolar and starburst inputs to DSGCs, the E/I ratio is predicted to change over the duration of directional light responses (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The model indicates that the effect of changing E/I ratio is most pronounced during slow stimulus velocities, leading to a deterioration of DS.
source: Our model indicates that this effect is most pronounced during slow stimulus velocities, as temporal offsets caused by spatial differences are exacerbated as more time is spent between activations of each input to the DSGC, leading to a deterioration of DS (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling described in the manuscript, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In real DSGCs, DS is stable across velocities, indicating that there must be additional mechanisms that compensate for the effects of changing E/I ratio.
source: However, in real DSGCs, DS is stable across velocities (Brombas et al., 2017), indicating that there must be additional mechanisms that compensate for these effects (e.g. inhibition from non-DS sources).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and previous research.

claim: The realization of multiple DS mechanisms helps settle divergent views on whether timing or amplitude ratios generate DS in ganglion cells.
source: In the case of pinpointing the mechanisms generating direction selectivity in starbursts (Ding et al., 2016; Fransen and Borghuis, 2017; Kim et al., 2014; Lee and Zhou, 2006; Münch and Werblin, 2006), or understanding whether timing (Koch et al., 1982; Taylor et al., 2000; Torre and Poggio, 1978) or amplitude ratios generate DS in ganglion cells, the realization of multiple DS mechanisms helps settle divergent views.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The suggestion of a central role for starburst ACh in driving E/I temporal offsets necessitates re-enquiry into previous results which indicated a modulatory role.
source: In contrast, the suggestion of a central role for starburst ACh in driving E/I temporal offsets, necessitates re-enquiry into previous results which indicated a modulatory role.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: DS neurons in higher visual areas may also be created using a variety of circuit mechanisms.
source: Given the multiple DS mechanisms in the retina, it is interesting to speculate that DS neurons in higher visual areas are also created using a variety of circuit mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Thalamocortical inputs to the visual cortex exhibit strong DS properties, apparently with retinal origin.
source: For example, thalamocortical inputs to the visual cortex exhibit strong DS properties (Sun et al., 2016), apparently with retinal origin (Cruz-Martín et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Abolishing retinal direction selectivity has modest effects on cortical DS, indicating that direction selectivity must also arise de novo through alternate parallel mechanisms.
source: Yet, abolishing retinal direction selectivity has modest effects on cortical DS (Hillier et al., 2017), indicating that direction selectivity must also arise de novo through alternate parallel mechanisms (Lien and Scanziani, 2018; Saul et al., 2005; Wilson et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In primate visual cortex, distinct mechanisms appear to shape early and late response similar to what was observed for DSGCs, suggestive of a common organizational principle.
source: Strikingly, in primate visual cortex, distinct mechanisms appear to shape early and late response (Pack and Born, 2001; Thiele et al., 2004) similar to what we have observed here for DSGCs, suggestive of a common organizational principle.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Direction selectivity in other sensory areas including the auditory and somatosensory systems may also rely on temporal and amplitude E/I asymmetries.
source: It is also interesting to note that direction selectivity in other sensory areas including the auditory and somatosensory systems (Kuo and Wu, 2012; Wilent and Contreras, 2005) may also rely on temporal and amplitude E/I asymmetries (Li et al., 2015; Ye et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is only through the marriage of anatomical and physiological approaches can the circuit mechanisms be fully realized.
source: While large-scale ultrastructural circuit mapping is bound to reveal circuit elements involved in the computation, it is only through the marriage of anatomical and physiological approaches can the circuit mechanisms be fully realized, as we have demonstrated here for the generation of direction selectivity at multiple levels in the mouse retina.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.
